title: Research
text: Our research sits at the intersection of vascular neurology, neurointervention, and data science. We use electronic health records, multicenter registries, imaging, and wearable sensors to answer practical questions in stroke prevention, treatment, and recovery.

title: Research
section: Peri-procedural stroke: predicting risk before it becomes harm
text:
Peri-procedural stroke: predicting risk before it becomes harm


Perioperative stroke is uncommon overall but disproportionately affects patients undergoing cardiac, major vascular, and neurosurgical procedures. Our work combines clinical synthesis with patient-level prediction.
In 2026, we published an EHR-derived model using 255,850 procedures for derivation and 189,095 procedures for external validation. The model used routine clinical and procedural information and achieved an external-validation AUC of 0.86, separating patients into clinically useful risk strata.
Open the risk calculator ↗ · Read the validated model · Read the 2025 review in Stroke

title: Research
section: Clinical AI: turning free text into research-ready evidence
text:
Clinical AI: turning free text into research-ready evidence


Stroke registries depend on labor-intensive chart review. In a completed multicenter study, we evaluated 22 open-source language models on 2,416 neurointerventional reports from patients treated for large-vessel-occlusion stroke.
The best model reached 94.8% overall extraction accuracy across eight clinically relevant variables and aligned more closely with expert interpretation than non-expert annotation for seven of eight variables. This work demonstrates a practical route to scalable, secure registry curation without custom preprocessing.
Read the 2026 study in AJNR



Best model


94.8%

Overall accuracy in structured chart abstraction

title: Research
section: Cerebral venous thrombosis: treatment and long-term risk
text:
Cerebral venous thrombosis: treatment and long-term risk


Through international multicenter collaborations, we have studied anticoagulant treatment, recurrent thrombosis, and epilepsy after cerebral venous thrombosis (CVT).
The DIAS³ study developed a simple six-variable score and validated it in two independent cohorts. It estimates individualized 1- and 3-year epilepsy risk after CVT, supporting patient counseling and more personalized follow-up. Earlier ACTION-CVT work found that direct oral anticoagulants had comparable effectiveness to warfarin, with a lower risk of major hemorrhage in the primary multicenter analysis.
Open the DIAS³ calculator ↗ · Read the DIAS³ study · Read ACTION-CVT

title: Research
section: Cervical artery dissection: treatment, recurrence, and population trends
text:
Cervical artery dissection: treatment, recurrence, and population trends


Completed nationwide and international studies have examined thrombolysis, recurrence, and changing incidence of cervical artery dissection.
Our 2025 nationwide analysis found that intravenous thrombolysis was associated with better odds of home discharge without a significant increase in intracerebral hemorrhage or in-hospital death. Separate work characterized US incidence trends and factors associated with recurrent stroke after dissection.

title: Research
section: Neurorecovery: measuring what the affected arm actually does
text:
Neurorecovery: measuring what the affected arm actually does


Wrist accelerometers record movement, but conventional counts cannot reliably distinguish purposeful activity from nonfunctional motion. In completed work with stroke survivors, our best intrasubject machine-learning model reached 92.6% accuracy and closely tracked expert video annotation.
This line of work reflects a broader interest in pairing motion capture, imaging, and computational methods to make recovery measurement more sensitive to real-world function.
Read the study in Neurorehabilitation and Neural Repair



Best intrasubject model


92.6%

title: About the Shu Lab
text: The Shu Lab is based in Pittsburgh and works across UPMC and Brown collaborations. We study stroke prevention, neuroendovascular outcomes, cerebrovascular epidemiology, clinical AI, and recovery through a translational, team-science approach.

title: About the Shu Lab
section: About Liqi Shu
text:
About Liqi Shu
Liqi Shu, MD, is a vascular neurologist at the UPMC Stroke Institute, core faculty in Pitt Cerebrovascular Medicine, and an Adjunct Instructor in Neurology at Brown University. He completed neurology residency and vascular neurology fellowship at Rhode Island Hospital/Brown, followed by the 2024–25 NIH StrokeNet SPIRIT research fellowship and neurointerventional training at UPMC.
His background in computer science and biology shapes a program that treats clinical data, imaging, language, EEG, and human movement as complementary signals. The lab’s completed work spans validated peri-procedural stroke prediction, large-language-model chart abstraction, international cerebrovascular registries, and machine-learning measures of post-stroke arm use.
Dr. Shu received a 2023 Brown Dean’s Excellence Award for teaching and mentoring in the Neurology Clerkship.

title: About the Shu Lab
section: Our principles
text:
Our principles


Start with the clinical need
The strongest analytic question begins with a decision patients and clinicians actually face.


Match the method to the question
We combine real-world evidence, registries, imaging, and quantitative models without treating any one method as the answer to everything.


Build collaboratively
Clinical insight, statistical rigor, engineering, and trainee curiosity are all part of the work.


Aim for translation
We favor outputs that can become better risk estimates, workflows, tools, and ultimately better care.


Explore our research

Profile information is linked to current institutional pages. Research claims on this site link to the corresponding peer-reviewed publication.
